_source: docs/content-bible.md §4 (Ancient lore surfaces), §6 (towns + aging arcs), §7 (gym leaders), §8 (story spine), §9 (side quests), §10 (NPCs), §13.13 (dialogue budget) + build-doc §15 C7. Names of species, places, people and organisations are transcribed from the bible, never invented (G2). GIVEN NAMES are the standing exception: the bible asks for quest and background NPCs without naming them, so their given names are coined under bible §10's naming convention — a coined given name is not a transcription error and must not be "corrected" back to a bible name.
_guardrail: G7 — no moralizing copy about catching, anywhere. NPCs state facts, express their own livelihood interests, and disagree with each other. No line tells the player they did wrong, implies guilt, or delivers a lesson. Enforced by the pattern scan in tests/unit/dialogue.test.ts and, because a regex cannot detect tone, by a line-by-line human-style read.
_budget: bible §13.13: ~10 lines per named NPC, ~3 per ambient, roughly 400–500 total. Shipped: see _counts. Named speakers that carry an Ancient lore chain or a six-act arc (Maren, Wick, Sel, Bram) run above 10; ambient speakers in the vertical-slice towns run above 3 because they carry year/population state variants the flat budget did not price in.
_conditionModel: An entry fires when every clause of `when` holds. TWO INDEPENDENT CLOCKS (Q3, the authorised L8 amendment): act/actMin/actMax are the STORY clock and every story beat gates on them, so it fires whenever the player earns it, in any calendar year; years/yearMin/yearMax are the WORLD clock — unbounded, never waiting for the player — and only world-ageing copy reads it. THE ACT LADDER IS core/acts.ts actOf(), which is the repo's only act authority and reads data/balance.json acts.gates: acts run 0..6, and ACT 0 IS THE PROLOGUE — a real state every new save starts in, which act 1 opens on story.opening.done. An `act` EQUALITY closes the entry the moment the act advances, so it is used only where the beat belongs to that act and nowhere else (the prologue; each act's arrival greeting); anything a player can walk past and come back to uses actMin, because town N's gym and route N unlock in the same act. seasons gate the four migrant windows; flagsSet/flagsUnset/flagEquals read SaveFile.questFlags; population/floraStock read the LIVE node state (SaveFile.nodeStates), so a town's lines change as its web does — a line that quotes a count or an abundance must carry the clause that makes it true. Among the entries that match a (speaker,node,kind) request the game takes the highest `priority` (default 0). Every greeting/ambient group ships an unconditional fallback, so a matching entry always exists.

_chains.vellsire-chain: bible §4 'Maren's keystone lectures' + 'Duskhollow astronomers on the Vellsire's vanishing'. Steps 1..11 alternate NPC and antler-standing-stone props across Hearthollow → r1 → Brackwater → r2 → r3 → Bowerdeep → Cindershelf → Duskhollow (Orrin) → sanctum-approach → sanctum. Each step is gated on the previous step's flag, so the lore opens as it is earned rather than arriving as one block.
_chains.undermere-chain: bible §4 "Sel's serpent tales". Steps 1..7 alternate Sel and the sunken idols at brackwater/r2; step 5 additionally requires the Ferryman's Wager (bible §9) to be finished. Completing it sets chain.undermere.complete, the gate on the Undermere hunt.
_chains.kilnback-chain: bible §4 'Bram and the miners on the warm shell below'. Steps 1..6 alternate Bram, the miner Gerta and the shell-kiln shrines in the Cindershelf mine. Completing it sets chain.kilnback.complete, the gate on the Kilnback hunt.

lines.text: You came up here looking for work and there's work going, so you're taken on. The pay is poor and the walking is most of it. There's more ground out there than one person gets round in a season.
My name's Maren. Warden for the region, and it's been the one post since they made it.
There was a keystone animal here once. The Vellsire, a stag. The last of that herd went out of Fallowmere about thirty years back, and the ground up here has been without them ever since.

Three in the pen behind you. A Cindril, a Puddlisk and a Thornlet, all of them out of this spring. A young one has about three years of work in it, and after that it comes back here and lives on without working.
Have a proper look at all three, because I can't swap it over afterwards.
The Cindril, then. Fire animal, and the quickest of the three by a long way.
It'll be a Vulkindle at two and a Pyrevane at three, and it's the same animal the whole way through with a new name on the card. Bring it down each time and I'll weigh it for you.
The Puddlisk, then. Water animal.
The skin's clear enough to watch its dinner go down inside it. Rillisk at two, Maelstrisk at three. They go over in the night, so you come down to something bigger with a different name on the card.
The Thornlet, then. Plant animal. It'll open your forearm up if you carry it against your chest, so use the crook of your arm. Bramblore at two, Thornwald at three.
Same animal each time, only bigger. By the third year you'll not lift it.
Snares first. Three of them, in the satchel by the door. The satchel comes back to me.

One snare holds one animal long enough for you to get your hands on it. After that there's one fewer where you took it from. Bait makes a snare likelier to hold, and you make the bait out of whatever the animal eats.
A base one lets go of anything that fights hard, and a weighted one holds. The smith sends them up when he has the iron for it. Keep the weighted for whatever's already put a team down.
And this is the survey board. Every place in the region down one side. What's living there is written against the place, and a number against that.
Most of what's on it is mine. That's why it reads three weeks out of date anywhere north of the gate, and further behind than that up on the steppe.
So read it on your way out of the north gate and again on your way back in. Take four of the Nibbin off Meadow Reach and the board reads four fewer when I write it up that evening.

One more thing before you go far. There'll be tracks out on the Reach. You'll see droppings too, and a flattened patch where something's lain up. Read one and you'll know what came past and roughly when.
Some things are only here part of the year. Pollywisp are a spring animal on the Reach, so a card you read on one in autumn comes back dormant. And a dull animal reads nothing off a good clear track.
Walk Meadow Reach and write me three cards.
Three cards. A Loamunder, a Nibbin, and one you weren't sure of. I'd put that down as Bramblehog.

Three more than I had for the Reach at the start of the week. There's a word you'll want off me before long, and it's keystone. I'm at the station most mornings and the board gets written up before eight.
One more thing about the snares. They work the other way round as well, which is the half people don't get told. You can open one and let the animal back out.
Whatever you let out goes into the ground or the water you're standing on.

Not back where you caught it. A release goes on the board the same way a catch does, only the number goes up instead of down. Hetty has wanted somebody putting Boglings back since spring and she'll be glad of you.
The Loamunder turn the soil, and I'd put a fair bit of the green out on the Reach down to that. That's a guess, mind, and not a walked one.
The green's holding up out there this year and I'd not have said so in the spring. Maribel keeps the gym at the bottom of the green, and it's the old Nibbin that will take some shifting.
Odo has the gym out on the east stilts. Three weeks since I was over at Brackmarsh, and it rained every day of it. What I've got written for that marsh is short of what's in it.

The silk and the timber come off the same trees here, and the two trades want different things off them. What's on my board for it is Vesper's, and I have not been over her figures. Two years since I walked this canopy properly.

Gerta has the steppe survey and can't walk the whole of it alone, which is why I'm asking. She's at the third shaft head most mornings and below the shaft the rest of the week. Nine months since I was up there myself, and it shows in what I've got written down.

Orrin's shelves go back further than anything I keep, and I've been up there every morning this week instead of walking the vale. He'll read the whole page out to you rather than tell you what's on it.
The gate is standing open. It has not been open in my lifetime and it was not me that opened it. The crows on this approach want counting before noon and I've not started.
You asked what a keystone is.
It's an animal that a great many other things turn out to depend on, far more than you'd guess from how few there are. Take one out and everything shifts about after it, slowly.

Some go up, some go down, and none of it shows on paper for four seasons. The ground came back richer the next year where the Vellsire herd grazed, and three people who didn't know each other wrote that down separately.
You read one of the stones out on the Reach, and there are more of them than that one.
I've walked to three of the others myself this season. The rest I have off Orrin. He has them off a surveyor's letter, and I'd want to walk them before I said anything about them.
Whoever cut them was keeping a tally. The ones that still have a face carry the same six figures. The herd has not passed in thirty years and the stones go back a good deal further than that.
The felling crews let me at a fresh stump when I ask, and I've had forty-odd off them. You can read a tree's years off a stump: a wide ring is a fat year, a thin one is a poor year.
Every one of those forty reads wide, wide, wide, and then thin to the bark.

The thin starts within a season of the last time anybody wrote down seeing a Vellsire. One stump like that is a bad tree. Forty like that and I still can't call it anything. I would rather say so than guess.

There's less green up on that steppe than there is on the Reach. A place empties from the bottom up: green goes first, then whatever lived on the green, and whatever was at the top goes last and has been hungry a long while by then.
What I can tell you about that steppe is Gerta's work, because I have not been up there since the thaw.
Four days I've been up at Orrin's shelves, and what I wanted off them was not the total.
I wanted to know who took each entry and where they were standing. Thirty years of those nights carry nothing in the margin at all.
Not one of those hands put down the hour, or the weather, or whether they went out looking or just happened to be at the window. Figures like that I can use. What I cannot do is put a season on them.
The Sanctum Fallow was shut before those stones were cut, and fallow is a farming word. It means ground you've left to rest on purpose, so somebody shut it and meant it to come back.
If the herd went anywhere it went in there.

There'll be no herd left to find, though. One animal at the outside, and an old one. What you do standing in front of it is yours to decide. It'll be a long while before it shows in anything I can measure.
The animal's out of working years. It's come to the end of what it had in it, and there's nothing wrong with it otherwise.

Two things can come of this. You can have a young one out of the same stock, carrying one or two of the things this one was good at. Or something you've already got gets better at one thing for good, in this one's name.

It'll be down at the station from tomorrow. Fed, with the run of the yard, and no work at all for the rest of its life. The yard is fed at four and it has been fed at four every year I have been walking.

The west scarp has carried three big Stonewing every year I've had this job, and Gerta walked it five days back and found one. It may have gone the usual way. The Cragmar and the Ashvole would have thinned out first, then the Pyrelisk that feed on the Ashvole.
I can't tell you yet that that's what happened. A bird that size feels it last of all.
Greaves went through the gate an hour ago, on foot.
I'll be up on the rim with the board. A morning's work still on it.

You'll be Maren's, then. The one she's got walking the Reach for her. I'm Wick, second year with the Cullbrand Company, and this route's on my intake sheet. Company pays by the head and doesn't ask whose.
I'm grade four. Eleven a head.
The bird's a Carricrow. Down as common on the sheet, and it pays like it.
Five to four on the last exchange, and the returns sheet gets that figure tonight. It'll say I lost. That's the whole use of a returns sheet. I'm on the marsh road tomorrow either way.
I've a room over the net loft, a column to fill, and I'm still grade four.

You had the better of me by less than the returns sheet will make it look, and I'll say so on the sheet. You've walked the whole Reach for her. Cullbrand puts one man on half of it and calls that a route, and that man is on four.
Brackwater's whole fishery is priced off the Fenmaw, and has been for sixty years. It's in the intake schedule and I can show you the page.
Same schedule as my first week, and I was grade four when I first read that page. Down here it goes by the season, and half the town eats off it.
I went early. I always go early out here. Sel poles the channel crossing at the far end and he'll take you over for the rate on his post.
Two exchanges out here, and you're on nobody's books. I'm on five.

Intake issues a tide table with the slack twenty minutes late on this stretch, and I went on the table. There is a corrected one in the building somewhere and it has not reached my sheet. I went in on the water that table gave me, and the sheet will show five.
First thing. I had the fishery wrong. It's priced off the channel and it always was.

The buyer took the contract off his shelf and made me read the clause out in front of two other men. They put me up to grade six the same week. My buyer list now has a name off every house on all three levels.
I've checked. Maren doesn't pay you and you're not on anybody's books, and I am on six.
You're not ours and here you are anyway. I put a query in to intake and the answer came back blank. They filed the blank.
Three years running and you've had me every time. If you were ours, you'd be up two grades by this afternoon — level with me at six.

There's a clause in the wilds contract. It puts a Company man on a marked stand a fortnight before anybody else. I've had this stand fourteen days longer than you have, and the clause is numbered nine.
You've walked the steppe. I worked it.
Two seasons on the west scarp with a Cullbrand crew, and I took the bonus. Cullbrand paid out on Cinder Steppe for four years, and there were families in four towns eating off that money.
The scarp went empty in the fifth year. It paid for part of my move from grade four to grade seven, and I am on seven.
Bram keeps the forge under Cindershelf and does relic work. My first Carricrow aged out two winters back and he set the relic off it into this harness.
Not much left standing on this scarp, and you came off it with a team on its feet.
The salvage crew is down there till dark. Take the walk down if you want. Beaten on a dead scarp, and still on seven.
Greaves gave me his argument once, in a corridor. The animals belong to nobody, somebody will take them, and the money paid for the vale road.
Two years I've looked for the answer to that. Grade eight now, and no answer. If you find it, say it to me before you say it to anybody on nine.
I could put in for a transfer tomorrow and they'd sign it inside the week. Two men at intake have asked for the vale already and both got it. I'm not putting the form in yet.
I want to beat you first. Then I'll put the form in.

I'll not give you a reason for that one. Wispurr all over this ground since the winter, and I lost it anyway. There's a transfer form on my table with the vale written in and the date on it left blank, and I am still on eight.
There's a thing up on rollers past the gate stone and I've seen the build sheet. It's rated to carry the weight of a barge.
I'm not going in with him.

I was on the steppe crew for a last draw once, so I know what the column looks like the season after. There is nothing under it at all, and nobody above me has looked at that page since the payout cleared.

The office will say I've gone soft. I did the sums anyway, on Company paper, in my own time. What the Company has that animal valued at, and what's left once it's gone. Beat me first, and then go up the road and put the whole of it to him yourself. I'm on nine and I have nothing to add after nine.
Every one of those six years is written up in the returns, whichever way it went. My first year's sheets are still in a box at intake with my own hand all over them.
The way up past the gate stone is clear and there's a man posted. His rate on the build sheet is nine.

Then I'll be here a while longer, and that suits me. I'm in no hurry at all to be the one who walks in through that gate behind Greaves. The office knows where I am. I am at the gate stone with my sheet and still on nine.
A barge three days late, a buyer who won't sign till he's seen it, and the standing charge comes off my column and not off theirs.
Invoices are half this job. The other half is standing about waiting on them, and I'm on five.

You will have been told a good deal about the Cullbrand Company, and very little of it will have been accurate. I am Greaves, and the Bowerdeep accounts are mine, which is why I am standing in a night market at this hour.

Cullbrand does not log Bowerdeep and never has. Cullbrand buys timber and finished silk from parties who log Bowerdeep, under contracts drafted by people I pay well, and my lawyers regard that distinction as material.

Maren has you counting, I understand. We keep something of the same sort. Ours is called an inventory, it is audited in the spring and again in the autumn by people engaged to find it wrong, and it balances to the individual animal.
She is doing that work with a notebook and no staff.
Cinder Steppe was let to Cullbrand on a six-year contract. The schedule was met in four. The board took the view that finishing ahead of schedule was good management, and against the schedule it was.
Nothing else was being measured. I am told the company store shut in the week the crew were paid off. This town had four years of wages out of that contract and nothing since.
There are men on this street who ate better under that contract than in any year after.
You have been counting for the warden for six years, and she has your figures. I have no quarrel with the figures. My own people would have arrived at much the same numbers eventually, and later.
A man I employ put it to me in writing that they would have been later, and it is minuted.

The animal in that ring belongs to nobody. The board takes the view that an animal of that size with no owner is an asset this Company is entitled to acquire. You are standing between the ring and the teams on the rim. Instructions have gone to the teams. They are waiting.

The afternoon has gone to somebody who walked up here on foot, and I would like that entered accurately, which it will not be. I have forty years of records and not one page about a region after a contract closed.
The animal is behind you. The teams on the rim have been paid and dismissed.

The result has been entered and the schedule is not affected by it. It has not changed the view I took of you when we first met, which was favourable. Come back up when you are ready. The teams are paid to the end of the week, whatever is decided.
Bramblehog first, then the Skir. Then Old Nib.
The notice on the door still says four, and it has since the bad winter.

The Bramblehog's hand-reared off my own line and never learned to keep off a person, so she comes in low and leans. Old Nib is twelve this spring and I've not seen her hurry in four years. She waits where she stands, and there's not much gets through a pelt of that age.

Old Nib's feet want doing tonight and she'll not stand for it without somebody at her head, so I'm an hour in that shed. Come the turn of the year the whole green goes up in lanterns and we feed whoever walks in.
Badge is in the apron pocket. Hold on. There you are.
Old Nib's still on her feet, so she'll stop out on the yard tonight the way she does when she's won. Her supper goes out at four and she'll not come in off that yard till morning.
The Skir only come in over my hedge three and four at a time when the Reach has gone short on the other side of it. I've had a bucket out at the gatepost all week and they'll take it out of my hand.
Meadow Reach has gone thin on Nibbin. Mine are penned and hand-fed and I've not lost one.
I'm in and out of the shed all morning, so speak up when you want me.

One of the Bramblehog's off her food. Mouth open, feet up, sound at both ends. The other got through the hedge into the barley after the Loamunder. Two Bramblehog, two jobs, and neither is Old Nib. My morning's the barley and my afternoon's the hedge, and I've lost none.
Hold on. — That boat's coming in wrong on the far stilts.
Right. Bogling first, then Reedrick. Whose boat is that.
Sit down. That bench is Sel's and it holds. Fenmaw's last out, and she's big, and she comes up slow. Twenty minutes to the slack yet, maybe more. We go on the slack and not before it.
Good fight. — The small ones now. Bogling, we call them at that size. They eat the same Reedrick the big ones eat, only smaller Reedrick, and I've had the one animal in my hands at both sizes.
Badge is in the tin by the door. Take it out yourself, my hands are wet. — Whose boat was that, in the end.
I'm out on the water till the light goes. Two hours to the slack yet, near enough. The slack brings me in and nothing else does.
Hetty has the shallows figure and hers is better than mine. The fishery pays less when the marsh is short, so the men on the stilts are on a bad week for it.
Brackmarsh has gone quiet on Mirefin. Hold on. The ebb's starting.

There's more Sporantle in this marsh than anything else and no buyer for one of them. They sit up against the reed edge and they don't shift about. Same yard of water two days running and you'll take another.
The far bank's out further than it was in the spring. Two foot of it, near enough, and still going.
Halder wants three Webvern out of the Wilds canopy, full-grown, and his buyers are contracted.
A canopy that size carries eight, near enough. From the ground, with a glass, in the last week of summer, and walked by me.

His order is a real one and I have said so at the council table. The old Webvern is last off my bench and she will get her toxin into whatever is standing when she comes out. What happens here goes up on the board tonight, dated.

The old Webvern got her toxin into you and it hardly showed at the first exchange. It goes on building after that. By the sixth it is taking a real piece out of whatever is standing, and nothing shakes it off once it is in.
Badge is yours. My figure and yours both go up on the board tonight, written, dated and signed.

Your animal is quicker than she is and it made no difference, because she gets her strike in the moment she is out. Nine times in ten the first strike is the one that matters. She is on her own speed after that.
The Barkhide browse the understory back hard, and the light down here is on their account.
Halder pins his order up on the market board. My own figure goes up beside it, with the date on it.
Ashvole. Cragmar. Then the warm one, second Ashvole. Stonewing. Pyrelisk.
Six on the bench. Take as long as you want, and take your coat off first.
Last one's a Pyrelisk as well. Older. Off the west vents. Two seasons, that one took.
The Stonewing doesn't mind the wet. Most of the rest of that bench goes out the moment it gets wet. Bram's through the back, past the slag heap.
Here. Your badge. He takes relics gone brittle, not cracked.
Bench is still warm. I'm not banking it down yet. My forge is the small one, thirty feet that way. Give the door a good bang. A soft knock won't carry.
Ground's warm under the west path. Warm since the last flare. Gerta's at the head of the third shaft most days.
Colder up there than down here. Wear a coat.
Room's dark. It stays dark. Bring a lamp for the walk down.
The Duskstalk wakes last. They go out in the order they wake.
Mine stop a thing where it stands. There was a woman here before me. She left the Duskstalk. I have fed it since.
You got through the Duskstalk. Three have done that. Two still come up in winter.
Badge. — Gate's off the vale road. A mile past the last light, and nobody uses it much.
The door's not locked. It is the same dark at noon. They wake in the same order whatever hour you come.
The Carricrow came into the vale a few years back. They settle where things have died. Children up here feed them bread by hand.
Dark at four here in winter. Under the rim it goes earlier still.
Rates are on the post. They don't move for the rain and they don't move for the sun.
Forty-one years on this crossing. I've been late the once. That was my brother's wedding, and he's sixty-eight now and he still — right, sit yourself down, we're going.
Across, then. The fare's on the post. Sit in the middle of the boat, and your hands stay inside it.
Crossing, or the crossing and the stories? Same money either way. The stories are free.
The story starts with my pole and you're welcome to measure it, ten feet near enough, and anywhere along my crossing it finds bottom at five feet or six.
In four places it doesn't. I've looked for a fifth all my life.

The whole ten feet goes down and there's still nothing under the end of it. My grandfather marked those four and I mark the same four, only I shifted one of his a foot east. Two have a stone figure sunk on the rim, and the near one shows off the dock at low water.
So you've had a look at the figure off the dock rim. That stone is not marsh stone. I had a mason down one summer and he couldn't place it.

My grandfather called the four places the lake-beneath-the-lake. He meant a second water under ours, and the four are where the two meet. Every other stretch of this channel silts up, and in my lifetime those four have not taken a foot of mud.
You'll see it off the dock at half tide, and at half tide only, because at low water the light comes off the mud and goes wrong on it.
You got your Mirefin inside the year, so the rest of the tale's owed you. The barge is due in, so you're hearing this one on your feet.

The figure is eyeless. The face is finished everywhere else, mind. Where the eyes should be, there was never anything cut at all. My grandfather said whatever's down there came up the once, in a flood year, and the town felt it through the pilings.
He'd never say what he saw. They're bringing the plank over, so mind your feet on it.
So you've been out to the second figure, the one in the reeds.

The pair of them now, facing each other across two miles of reed, and whoever cut the one cut the other. Draw a line between them and it runs right over the third of my four places. I don't leave the boat sitting over that place.
You'll want something with you that can swim. Slack water is the time for it, and an hour either side is no good to you.
Here. My grandfather's card, and mine underneath his on the same string. There's spare string for a third, and nothing of mine to put on it.
The name on the older card is Undermere. The writing is nothing like my grandfather's.
He told me the card was older than the town. It says the thing down there does not age. I don't know what to do with a sentence like that. He believed it, and he was no fool about this water.
Third place, off the Brackmarsh figure, at slack water, and the evening barge is in at six and I'm on the dock for it.

A wager, then, while you're crossing anyway. An Elder Mirefin, out of the channel, back to this dock before the year turns. A big old one out of the deep, and none of your young ones out of the shallows.
An old one has one year of work left in it and no more than the one.

I say that out loud before anybody takes it. I keep my fare if it doesn't come off, same as any other day. Win and you cross free as long as I'm poling this boat. I'm sixty-six, so that's the size of what I'm putting up.
Deep edge of the channel, out where it runs. You'll not do it off the reed side.
An old one holds station out there and lets the current bring its food down. My grandfather baited for them with a Reedrick, because Reedrick is what they eat.
Fair enough. The offer keeps. If I'm not at the post I'm somewhere out on the crossing.

Comes of holding station in the channel and taking what comes down. Free crossings from here on, and I'll tell the lad on the second boat as well. There's the rest of the tale owing you whenever the barge isn't in.
A big one, and heavy with it. There's a jaw and a half on her.

Third piling's soft, fourth's going the same way, and nobody's driving new ones. Pilings come out of the levy, the levy comes off what the boats bring up out of the channel, and they're bringing up next to nothing.
I wrote to the harbourmaster in the spring and he wrote back agreeing, and anyway, the third one still wants minding on the way up.
The levy came in over what the board had budgeted and they put the extra into the dock. The deck's level enough to roll a barrel down it now, and they've done the same over at the second landing.
New pilings under three and four. I'd not have bet on it.
Mind your feet that side. Hot scale down there and it goes through a boot sole.
Ask away if it's the warm floor you've come about, only ask me while I'm working. The bellows are on your left. Wait for my nod before you pull and no sooner.
Put your hand flat on the floor. Go on. By the anvil, where the flagstone's worn smooth.

Warm, isn't it. My forge is cold till I light it after noon, so that's not where it's coming from. A vent comes up hot for an hour and then it's done with you, and this floor has never come up like that.
The men underground call it the warm shell below. Go up and look at the shrine at the shaft head.
You got up to the shrine, then. Take a candle next time and look along an edge where a plate's chipped. Those plates aren't cut stone at all. They're shell, every one, right through.
I had a broken piece on this bench a month and put it back in the scrap. Go and ask Gerta for her log.
Right. So you got down to the deep shrine.
Kilnback. The word cut on it, in the old letters. Somebody went into that reach and cut a name into a plate wider across than my doors, a long while before my father's father.
I've had my hand flat on that flagstone in every season there is and it comes up the same every time.
Go down when the vents are quiet. Take something at home in water or made out of rock, because nothing else will take a fire. Mind the last ladder, third rung's split.
So one of yours has aged out. You'll have the relic on you and it'll be warm still. I set it into a collar-piece, plain brass, and I cut the seat to the relic and not the other way about.
Bring it here and come back through the town tomorrow.
The young one that wears it carries some of what the old one had. How much, I couldn't tell you. It wants a day and a night in the ash. Don't come at me for it sooner.
There you are. Collar's cooled through and the seat's tight.

Get your thumb on the relic and try to shift it. It won't shift for you and it won't shift for me. Look underneath the strap while it's off the bench. The old one's name is cut in there, same as on all of them.
Fifth shaft's open as of this spring.
There's enough coming off the steppe to keep a crew fed while they dig, and Cragmar are grazing the high scarp again. My brother's lad has gone on the new shaft. Six days in seven he's on it.
Fourth shaft's boarded up. It didn't fall in. Nothing off that steppe these two seasons.
Somebody in an office signed a paper. I said my piece up at the office and they left the third open. Six days in seven I'm down it.
One reading a shift, off the wall of the third shaft, thirty-one years of it. Nobody's job when I started and nobody's job now.

The shift before mine kept saying the third was warmer than the fourth and I wanted to know if they had it right. Off the wall, mind — the air moves and the wall doesn't, so the air is no good to anybody.
Bram's sent you up for the log. One reading a shift, all of them mine, off the wall and not out of the air, and the same spot on the wall every time.
Eight over the fourth. Same depth, the two shafts. That's the only reason the two of them compare.
That eight has moved on two occasions in thirty-one years. It went to fourteen each time, four days at a stretch. Each time came after a summer with no vent flare.
Go down the warm reach before you take the log back. There's a shrine at the bottom, not like the ones at the shaft head. Put your hand flat on it and tell me what you get.
There's a survey wants doing up on the steppe and I'm below all week, so it can't be me that walks it.

Five I want numbers on. Ashvole, Cragmar, Pyrelisk, Stonewing, Carricrow, all of them up on Cinder Steppe. Hurry and you'll put the same Carricrow down in two places, because they won't settle anywhere for long.
And the west scarp. How far up the green gets now, measured off the old cairn. On your feet the whole day for that, and not a step of it worth hurrying.

West scarp first, then the vent line, then the low ground coming back — the order I walked it in, so your figures sit alongside my old ones. On a day when it's flaring there's nothing to be had off the vent line, so leave that part.
All right. It was a whole day I was asking for, and that's a lot to ask of somebody who's just walked in. Off shift I'm at the third shaft head, and there's no hurry on it from my side.
Carricrow first. They only settle where something's died lately, so a high Carricrow figure sends me straight to the other four.

Snell has it that the warmth off that scarp comes up out of the vents. I've read that wall one reading a shift since before the fourth shaft opened, same spot every time, and it has not moved. Whatever took the Stonewing off, it wasn't the ground.

Your five go in the log tonight, beside my old ones. The green off the cairn goes in the front, with how far up it gets and what the Ashvole and Cragmar graze off it. I want it in feet off the cairn, taken by you this morning, and I want it again from the same spot next spring.

Four fields, and one of them lies fallow every year whether I want it that way or not. It's the west field this year, and it was the west field two years back and all, which is not how a rotation's meant to run.
Mind the gate — lift and shove together or it stops dead. And the old gate was up by the pound, whatever Judd says.

The Loamunder work my west field for me. They go through the soil all season and the ground they've been through comes up better than the ground they haven't. They came on their own and they feed themselves.
Twenty-four my side of the fence. I counted them walking the field, week before last.

So: leave them alone till harvest, twenty-four still there when I walk the fence, and a share off the crop for you. Say it back to me if you like, because what I mean is twenty-four standing at harvest and the payment after the crop's in and not before.
Or take them instead. There are buyers in Hearthollow paying coin for a Loamunder today and I'd not stop you.

choices.text: Twenty-four, and I touch none of them.

lines.text: Good. Twenty-four now, twenty-four at harvest, and the share off the crop when the crop's in. Twenty-four when I walk that fence at the turn.
The Reach has its own Loamunder past the north gate. This arrangement is the twenty-four in my west field, and those on the Reach were never in it.
Fair enough. The offer stands till harvest and next year too. You can tell me either way. West field to settle before the frost and nobody but me to do it.
You've left me the twenty-four standing. Two out there are young ones that weren't there in the spring. Here's your share, and it came out heavier than I quoted you. So take the difference.
West field came in at full weight. It hasn't done that in three years.
Same arrangement next spring if you want it. I walk the fence at the turn.

I walked the fence this morning and came up under the twenty-four, so there's no share off the crop this year. We set it that way at the start. Some years the field carries them and some years it doesn't. There's tea in the house if you want it.
West field goes fallow another year, then. I'll sow the east heavier and make it up somewhere.
Offer's the same next spring if you want it then. And the fence gets walked at the turn whichever way you go.
The fishery cut me to half hours two seasons back, and I've had the mornings since.
I spend them in the shallows, and that board by the door is mine, all of it. Hetty, by the way, and I should have led with that. So the mornings are mine.
Here's what I want, and I'll be quick. Four Boglings put back in on the Brackmarsh side.
A Bogling turns into a Mirefin inside a year, so four in the shallows now is four in the channel next year, if all four live, which they won't. I ask four because I'd sooner have three than two.
Board by my door is where it goes. The chalk's damp on the third column because the door leaks. Read it in the light or you'll take the Brackmarsh column for the channel one.
Brackmarsh side, in the shallows, and you want to be stood in the water rather than leaning out of a boat. The tide's up over that bank within the hour.
Brackmarsh side. There's a Fenmaw works the channel mouth and it'll have a Bogling off you. You want to stay off the mouth. Then it's four on my board and three in the water.
The buyer pays on the channel. Only the channel. My mornings in the shallows are my own time and they have nothing to do with anybody's wage.

The levy comes off the buyer's price and pays for the pilings and the harbour wall. So a thin year in the channel and the dock doesn't get mended. Sel's your man for the pilings — he's had letters about those.
On the Brackmarsh side, four Boglings, and that's mine to ask.
Four, and I'll write four. I'll come back and rule the column to three if the Fenmaw at the mouth has one off them before the year's out. Chalk goes on before the damp gets at the board.
Four in. Brackmarsh column up by four.
Webvern silk takes a dye nothing else will take. A fifth of every bolt is mine, and that's my living.
Silk and thread here, and finished bolt if you want it woven already. What do I pay in? Coin, on the day.
You're after work? Then here's one — three Webvern, full-grown, alive, delivered to the winding house.

Now the awkward part. It comes with the terms rather than after them. Vesper has been at the council about this order all season. Her case is that three grown Webvern is more than that canopy puts back in a year.
We've argued it for years, a fair bit of it in her own kitchen.
I pay my price the day they reach the winding house, in coin and not in credit. Or go and hear Vesper out first, she's at the council table until dark.
Full-grown only. How do you tell? A young one spins a thread that pulls apart.

They hang in the high lines out in Bowerdeep Wilds, above where the loggers are cutting. Every one of the lads was bitten inside the first month, and I pay for the salve. Poisonous, the whole lot of them, and the young ones as much as the old.
Go and hear Vesper out, then. She's on the council side of the market until dark. She'll give you her figure down to the last one. That order stands till the barge goes, whichever way you come at it.
Three, full-grown, and the winding house has them off you already. Here's your money, today, in coin, the way I said. Vesper will have a new figure by the festival.
Bolt goes out on the morning barge. Where does my fifth come off? At the far end, not this one.
Keep left going out. Winding house to the stair and back.
Four out past the second bend tonight. Kit's in the box. Anyway.
Moths start tonight. Gloomoth, up out of the Wilds, through the town, and on to wherever it is they go.
They put the lamps out coming through. That many in the air at once and a flame won't hold. Every autumn I'm short-handed for it.
So. Somebody out to the eastern stair with me and back, one night, with the relight kit, while they're still coming through.
Duskstalk work the dark stretches. We go together or not at all.

choices.text: I'd rather not walk it in the dark.

lines.text: Stay on the lit stretch. Move when I move. Slow out, slow back. A lamp goes out and we stop. We don't move till it's lit.
I'll walk it dark, then. Done that plenty of years. The moths are through in a fortnight. Then there's no job till autumn. So.
Every lamp lit, out and back. Good walking. The Duskstalk turned at the stair and never came down the road. They won't come down a lit one.
Kit goes back in the box by the gate. The moths'll be gone by winter. I'll miss them. Anyway.
Two censuses in this building. The one overhead is the sky and belongs to everybody. The one on the ground is animals, and it is mine.
The ground one is kept to a written standard, and the standard is nailed up beside the door. I have amended that standard on two occasions and dated each one.

One card for every animal you have taken and kept. The Bogling gets a card and the Mirefin gets a card, one for every individual and not one for every species. Orrin files by species and calls mine fussy.
Bring me a name the census has not got and I will have a plate painted for it.
Dormant is not the same thing as migrating, and the card says which. Anything that goes away for part of the year has that marked on its card, and it has not gone.

Thirty-five names in the full census, and I am four short of the thirty-five. Three of the four are single animals. The fourth came in as a form, and a form gets a card of its own, because a form is not a name.
Hold the plate by the edge. The paint is still tacky.
I am sorry about the light. The lamp is four years old and Ives says the trouble is my eyes. Somebody could look at the lamp.
Through the arch on the left, and mind the step. The shelves are down here, and the ink on the near end is browner than it ought to be.
The vanishing. Yes. I can read you some of it, if you like.

The sky is logged here every night and has been since the observatory got its roof on. Anything that crosses the vale underneath the instrument goes in the margin of that night's page. A herd, a cart, a man with a dog.

There are two hundred and six margin entries for Vellsire in ninety years of pages. Herds of nine, of twelve, of four, almost all inside the same three weeks of the year. Then one entry in three different hands, all three describing a herd of six crossing toward the caldera.
After that night there is nothing more in the margin. I looked for a falling-off first and there is none to find. Thirty years of nights, and not one Vellsire in any of them.

The book does not have where they went. It only ever held what crossed the vale. The antler stones on the roads were standing long before anybody here kept a book, and somebody was going out and keeping them up for years after.

The stones stand in an order, and the mark on each points at the next along. Meadow Reach, then Brackmarsh, then the Wilds, then the steppe, then the vale, then the Approach. I copied that order out of a surveyor's letter of the sixtieth year.
The marks are cut in and shallow now, and mossed over where the stone lies flat.
Do not scrape at them. Take a copy of what you can read, and write down which ones you cannot. Walk the six in that order and bring me what each one says.

choices.text: I'd not get to the sixth this year.

lines.text: The sixth I would leave until last. It is the largest of them and it carries the herd on both faces, so walk round the back of it before you put your pencil away.
In order, if you can. The marks make very little sense to me if they are read out of turn.
No, no. That is quite all right. Come up when the six are walked. Take whatever order the year gives you. You can bring me the four you walked if the year gives you only four.
All six, and in order. Thank you. Sit down while I lay them out, in the order you walked them. Read across and they give a direction, and they give a season as well.
The walk over here is beyond me now.

The direction will not surprise anybody in this vale. It points at the Sanctum Fallow, and people here have said so for years with not one page behind it. This will have to go to Maren, the direction and the season both, since it will have to be her that walks up there and not me.
FIELD STATION — HEARTHOLLOW. Survey sheets go up at first light. Pencil and blanks in the tin by the door. Sign for the sheet you take, and sign it back in. Sheets are not to leave the parish.
Pencil underneath, a worse pen: north gate for the Reach. Smaller again: yes, and thank you. Under both, a column of initials.
FORAGE SIGN — MEADOW REACH. Four signs: tracks, scrapes, castings, browse line. MIGRATING is the season either side. DORMANT is further off than that.
Pencil under it, pressed hard: no sign and neither card, and it has gone off the Reach. Three hands have written that, and the last of them is mine.
One block of granite on the north rise, cut into branching antlers, taller than a person, set deep.
The turf has grown over the foot. The weather side is worn round and pale. A herd of six figures is cut shallow on the sheltered side, with a line running north out of them and off the edge.
The stone is warm to the hand where the meadow grass banks against the foot.
The southern stone is snapped off at about half its height. What is left is hooves and the bottom of a line, running north off the break.
The break carries the same lichen as the rest of the stone, at the same depth. There is no sign of the upper half along this rise or the next.
A stone figure stands in the water off the dock rim, turned out toward the channel. Only the crown of the head is above water, and the carving there is finished down to the parting in the hair.
The shallows round it are clear to the bottom, down to the weed and the stones lying there. The water directly under it is not, and the face does not come clear from the rim.
The water at the rim comes to a boot top. Six feet out, no bottom.
The second figure stands where the reeds thin, in shallower water than the one at the dock.
The eyes on this one were never cut.

It is turned back to face the dock figure, and the carving is the same so far as the dock figure can be seen at all. Between the two of them the reed stops growing in a band about a boat wide, and the water inside the band is darker.
The causeway stone leans downhill toward the water.
The peat has banked against the uphill side of it, about as high as a knee. The weather has taken the top of the carving away. Below that, six figures, and a line running east out of them.
The shallower cut runs its full length. The deeper stops before the edge.
NIGHT MARKET — open dusk to dawn. Silk, thread, dye, lamp oil, relight kits. Rent due the first night of the month, in coin.
Pinned under it on a scrap: the Webvern figure, midsummer. Eleven struck out, nine struck out, seven. Across it in ink: stop writing on my notice.

The forest has grown up around this stone. It is cut from the same granite as the stones out on the meadow. Two trunks stand hard against its sides, and both trunks have gone flat where they touch it.
The moss on the north face stops at a level line.

Six figures on the sheltered side, in the same order as the six on the marsh stone, with the line running east out of them. The bark is dead a hand either side where the nearer trunk has gone flat against the granite.
A low structure at the shaft head, built of curved plates fitted without mortar.
The plates have the colour of fired clay, and they are not clay. Up close the grain runs the way bone runs, fired hard enough to come out that colour, and each plate is thicker through than a door.
Candles have been set along the joins, and they have worn hollows into the plate underneath. Along the near join the hollows number nine, and along the far join four.
The second shrine stands at the bottom of the deep workings, past the last ladder. The air is still and a candle flame stands straight up.
The shrine is warmer than the rock it stands on. It has no joins anywhere: a single plate, shoulder height, curving away on both sides, with no tool mark on the outside.

A word is cut across the face, in a lettering the mine gave up using: KILNBACK. Inside the letters the plate is warmer to the hand than outside them. Below the letters the wax has built up and been cut back and built up again, and the cut marks number four.

Vent heat has glazed the windward face of this stone to a skin of glass, and the glass has crazed and lifted in patches the size of a hand. The sheltered face has none of that, and the cutting there is sharp.
Six figures on it, and the line out of them runs south-east. Ash lies thick out here, and none of it has caught in the cutting.
Most of this board is torn at the tacks. The printed half reads PLATES THIS YEAR and then the figure nine. A date under it, part torn.
The rest is later hands on the bare wood. One small: plates go out when the illustrators have time. Under that, harder: shelf hours on the door.
There is no sheltered side to this stone. It stands in open ground, with nothing higher than the grass for a quarter mile in any direction.
The cutting is shallow the whole way round. Six figures again, and the line out of them runs up the face and off the top edge instead of across it.

The gate stone is the largest on the road up, about double the height of the one out in the vale. It is set into cut rock rather than into ground. This stone carries the herd on both faces, and none of the others does.
On the outward face the six are walking in. On the inward face the same six are standing, and the hooves are cut level with the ground line.
A second stone stands further up the road. The antlers are roughed out to about half their depth, and one face carries no cutting.
Tools lie at the foot of it under the ash: a hammer and three wedges, side by side. The ash over them takes a boot in to the ankle, and none of it is broken.
Nine stones at the caldera heart, evenly spaced, every one facing in toward the middle. All of them are carved, and the carving on these is not a herd.
Each stone carries one animal on its own, cut to double the size of the figures on the stones outside. The grass inside the ring is short and even.
The grass elsewhere in the Sanctum Fallow stands to the knee. Inside the ring it has been grazed down level. The dung lying on it has not dried out.
The stag comes down into the ring from the high side of the caldera, and it does not hurry.
It is a Vellsire. The branching on its antlers is the branching cut on every stone from Meadow Reach up to here, and the spread is wider than a person is tall.
It stops in the middle of the ring, on the short grass, and puts its head up, standing side on to the rim about a snare's throw from where the path comes in.

You've got the stag, then. Let me look at it a minute. It's narrower through the shoulder than the drawings have it, and the near antler's been broken and grown back crooked. Held like that, it won't age another day.
The numbers, then. Meadow Reach, Brackmarsh, Bowerdeep Wilds, Cinder Steppe, Duskhollow Vale and the Approach, all six walked and counted this morning. Five by me and the steppe by Gerta.

With that animal held, the ground round the Sanctum and along the Approach holds at the rate it has held every year I've walked it. That's two young brought on, against the three it makes with the stag loose in there.
I'll put in the book that the snare held, and what was in it. The six figures go under it, with Gerta's name against the steppe one.
The stag went up the scarp and over the rim and out of sight. It stopped the once at the top, side on, long enough for me to see all of it. I had a pencil in my hand and never wrote a thing down.
The numbers, then. Meadow Reach, Brackmarsh, Bowerdeep Wilds, Cinder Steppe, Duskhollow Vale and the Approach, all six walked and counted this morning. Five by me and the steppe by Gerta.
With that animal loose, the ground round the Sanctum and along the Approach comes off that rate for the first time. That's three young brought on, against the two it has always made.
You were six years getting to it. In nine years somebody will ask me why the numbers moved, and I'd rather they had all of it from me.
Boots are by the fire, they were wringing wet, and the kettle's on. Don't start thanking me for either.

Your animals are in the byre with the door shut and that was done an hour since. A night here is half a season gone, so sleep out and keep the days if you're wanted before the turn. Room only, or supper as well?
The rooms are built out over the water on the stilts, so they move all night. The man in the end room last week told me flat he'd not shut an eye, and he was snoring through the floor by ten.
You'll say you won't sleep. They sway.
Day rate. We rent by the day because the night's when the market's open — four, five, six, linen. So it's the day rate, and it's now.
It's all in the one rate — feed, the yard, the fire, the lot of it — and I don't itemise. The key's on the hook at the stair, second door on the left — seven, eight, nine.
There's a tub going now, and the tubs fill straight off the hot spring. Whatever you've got with you comes out of that water better than it went in, and it costs nobody here a penny.
Vent side's warmer and it shakes. Other side's cold and it doesn't.
Shutters stay open. Top and bottom, all night, every room. Rule eleven, and the observatory wrote it, not me.

They had me read all twenty-two out loud before they'd let me sign. Third blanket's in the press if the room goes cold, which it will, because — shutters. That argument lives up the hill, and I'd walk it if I were you.
Snares and salve. Tonic's behind me and it costs what it costs.

Bait's in the crate by your knee, not sorted, so dig. The cheap sort's cut for a whole kind of animal at once, out of whatever that kind eats. The dear ones are cut for the one animal and cost three times the money.
The weighted ones want iron and the smith's had none since spring. One of those works out cheaper than a base one with a salve on top. He'll send some up when he has the iron and not before.
Reed bait's the bundle on the end of the trestle, and it has sat there since the thaw looking at me. There's nothing out on that marsh will look at it but a Reedrick.
And Reedrick come through in the summer, midsummer on if you want it exact.
Salve, though. Salve moves — everybody comes off that marsh cut about the hands. Tonic when I've got it in, and I've none this week. I put it down to the wet spring, same as the rest of it.
Night market. Dusk to dawn, and no, we don't do mornings.
Lamp oil, wicks, tonic, silk by the bolt — evening to you — silk by the bolt. I get master snares, two a year. If you want it honest, it was one last year, and two is the better number to say.
In the autumn a Gloomoth drops on that rail and the whole market steps round it. Up on that rail now there's one grazing the moss, and it hasn't noticed there's a stall under it.
Master snares went when the contract went and I've none coming.

Salve I have, and tonic when the cart brings it, which is not this month. There's nothing growing on this steppe to cut a proper bait out of, so it's the cheap sort or nothing. That will fetch a Cragmar as often as an Ashvole.
My prices went up the month next door boarded its windows, and they went up again the spring after, and prices are the prices.
Not that tin, that's for the wick. Fill's in the flat tin at the end.
Wispurr bait moves in the winter and not otherwise. It's in the drawer with the master snare, and that snare has been in there eighteen months.
The observatory buys its oil off the lampwright direct and walks past this door to do it. I don't ask why and I have stopped wondering about it.
You'll be off up the Reach, then. I drove cattle up there. Forty years of it, near enough, and we took them through the old gate down past the mill.

Grass does well up there. Always has. Which is — anyway, the Skir come over the hedge at dusk and hunt Nibbin out of the tussock, and I watched one drop and come up with nothing and go up and drop again twenty foot along.
There's a gate on your way through and the far latch drops if you don't lift it. Better gate was the one down past the mill. They moved it the year of the — no, it's gone.
The Reach has come up green right down to the fence line, and Tolm will get a crop off his west side in a year like this. His father had that field in oats. Or barley. It was the one or the other.
Tolm put it down to grass the first year. Or the second. I'd not swear to it.
The Reach is short this year. I'd have had the beasts down off that rise a month early.
The town fields go the way the Reach goes, and Tolm's west side goes first. That went first the year of the wet harvest and all, years before ever he touched the drainage down there.
Maren let me hold the survey book and I looked at every page of it and there isn't a single drawing anywhere in the whole thing.
My da says I'm not to keep on at her about it, and I am going to keep on at her about it.

There's a Nibbin under the mill step and her name is Kettle. I told Maren her name was Kettle, and she wrote her in as a Nibbin. I have looked at every page in that book for Kettle and she is not on any of them.
She's the same one and I'd know her anywhere. Maren wrote her in again at the turn and it still only says Nibbin. I can read that much now for myself.
Her face has gone white down the one side, and it was not like that before.
West gate's down again. Bramblehog, same post. It'll be back up before dark.
Loamunder go along under the west field all night, and I've ploughed that field top and bottom for four years and never turned one up.
Harvest is six weeks off and it's been dry all week. Four fields to bring in and the two hands you see.
A track's the easy sign. A browse line takes longer. It's where something's come along and eaten the tips off a bush and left the stems standing, and the bush is still stood there, mind. With me?
The stems are what I measure. A folding rule, notched down the side, off my mother.

Scrapes now. A scrape is bark rubbed off. Dug is different — dug leaves a cast, which is to say a little heap thrown out at the side of it. Pollywisp you'll not see before the spring, and the rest of the year they're down in the wet. Seen one?
Post's out of the ground down the west end, root and all.
Something comes through the wire there and takes it off with it. Cart gets to the second stile. I carry the rest from there, so that's a morning gone before I've started.
Warden wanted a number off me. I showed her the post. She wrote something down.
Barge alongside at slack, and slack's an hour off.
She'll not come in on a running tide, not with sixty ton in her. Mirefin out in barrels, flour and nails and rope in, and I've eaten out of every barrel that's crossed this dock.
You try putting sixty ton alongside on a running tide and tell me how precious you feel about it.
I keep off the third piling now when she comes alongside, because that is sixty ton of barge going onto soft timber every time she does it.
We're putting out half the barrels we did. No new piling will be driven this year.
Came alongside at slack and the deck never moved under her.
New timber on the third piling and the fourth, and it's the first these boards have had in eleven years. My boot still goes down in the place where the soft one used to be.
Coarse mesh for the grown Mirefin, fine for the Bogling. Summer mesh on the end rail for the Reedrick, and that one hangs dry three quarters of the year.
Water's colder than it was when I started, and that's all it is. The water's colder than it was when I started.
What comes up comes up smaller, and the mesh follows the water. It followed the water before me and it will do it after me. You'd not know that to look at a net.
Sel says don't trail your hand over the side. I do it anyway when he's poling.
Clause four says channel. Channel's the deep bit. It's why the boats go out where they go out.
My auntie Hetty went quiet at her supper when I said that. Then she said it back to me herself, only slower. And I said it after her again.
I'm not going to talk about my mother.
She cut the mark on my post. Second one past the steps.
The water comes up to that mark. It does not go over. Drought year, flood year, the same mark. My nephew has it that I cut a new one and forgot which. Where you are stood, the post is twenty steps.
I buy the season here for an office that is not in this town, and the schedule comes down in the first week of the year and I price against it.
Clause four says channel. It does not say shallows and it does not say marsh.

People bring me marsh figures every spring. Fenmaw take Mirefin, and Mirefin is the animal the contract is written on. So the marsh figures go in the file and I price off the channel. Clause four has not been amended in sixty years and it does not say marsh.
Mirefin come up thick with nothing taking them, and then the channel goes empty. There is a clause for that. It has been in the contract longer than I have, and it sets the price low.
The warden walked that marsh again last month and could not put a second Fenmaw in it.
The best week of my year, this. Third year I've come up for the picking.
The grass is four or five days further on than the same week last year, and the tussock's crept north on me as well, a hundred paces from the old edge to the new.
Wet springs, that'll be. There's an antler stone up on the north rise and it's where I stop for my dinner.
I walked the whole tussock this morning and turned up two Nibbin, and the same walk last year gave me a dozen before I got as far as the gate.
Skir are over the far hedge these days, so that rise is somebody else's ground now.

The same week last year the grass was no higher than my boot. The Nibbin have grazed that rise all week and there's grass standing yet. A Bramblehog on the path this morning hardly troubled to move for me.
The Reach has never come up this thick for me, and it's knee-high on the north rise.
Mind the wet plank. In you get, sit anywhere you like. She's steadier than she looks and no slower than his.
They stand on that bank a quarter of an hour waiting for Sel's boat rather than get in with me, and I have stopped minding that, or near enough.
Channel's on your left going out. Shallows on your right. The idol's out where the reed thins, facing the town, and I'll point it out as we're passing.
Reed's gone quiet. In the summer you'd not normally hear yourself out here.
The Sporantle are up thick on the mud, thicker than I have ever had them, and it all goes in the back of the fare book with the rest of what I see out here.
Give me a minute, I'm wedging this one and it'll go where I put it.
My back went two summers ago and I can still put a tree down exactly where I want it. The trouble is getting up off the ground after, and my wife has heard that one often enough to say it for me.
Below the town the Barkhide eat the low growth back to the dirt, and on ground like that a log walks down to the road one-handed.
No Barkhide on those slopes now, so the low growth has come right up. The young trees under it all came on in the one season, and the canopy is thinner than it was when we were cutting under it.
I've not had a saw out past the east stair in four years.
Grown Webvern silk I can tell through a glove. Both hands on a strand, pull as hard as I like, it holds. Young stuff comes apart on the frame while you're winding it.
Second grade. It doesn't leave here as anything else.
And the moths make none of it — the whole of it is Webvern work, off the adult line and nothing else.
You want the winding house? It's the — no, wait, are you going up the east stair, because I'm not allowed on the east stair.

Gloomgrub are the little ones, and they turn into the big ones out of the high lines. Only they don't, they're a different thing altogether. And then they come through and the silk comes off the wings and the lamps go out, whoomf.
A Gloomoth got down my collar and out of both hands — that's my sister up there —
Floor stair, was it? They all come up that way. On the walk we would have called that a floor matter, and on the floor they would have sent it up to the walk.
In my day a person knew which.

That was the lampkeeper's family who sent it up, his father before him and his father's brother as well, and I came up to the walk myself the year they re-cut the lower stair, which was the year after my father died. Or the year before it. Which of the two it was I could not now tell you.
First the lower run. Forty-one, forty-two, forty — no. I've lost my place. Start again.
Oil's in the shed behind the winding house. — Was it oil you wanted?
Pell has the stair. Mine's the walk, and mine is two hundred and eleven. In the autumn the Gloomoth put the lot of them out, and then it is two hundred and eleven again from the first lamp up.
Warm? Third's warm, aye. Hands know it before I'm off the second ladder, and that'll be the vents.
Pyrelisk? Up the vent line when it flares. Took the hair off my arm, the once.

Say that again this side of me — my left ear's been no good since the fourth shaft. Gerta's got the heat to the degree. She says it isn't the vents. I'd get the number wrong if I tried to give it you.
A vent opens and the ground round it goes soft. Soft ground is what we cut, so the housing went up behind the shaft, which is why the whole east row leans.
The shrines. We didn't put them there and we don't move them.

Ashvole burrow, and the cinder goes loose where they've been at it, loose enough to open a face and cost us a day off the cut with nothing paid for it. Nobody has got round to the loose bit down by the winch, and it has had a man over already.
Young men in good coats, in the front room, with a folder each.
One of them kept his gloves on indoors in high summer, in a room with a fire going in it, and I have never worked out why.

There were Stonewing on the west scarp when I was a girl, and Cragmar grazing the flat below them. Say they went in the third contract and that will be right. Say the second and I'd not argue with you over it.
The mine's boring.
There's a shrine bigger than a cart at the bottom of the third shaft, and I've not seen it and nobody's taking me down.
Sable's Pyrelisk is loud. Was that all you wanted? Only I was doing something.
The overalls are company issue and there's no company here to issue them.
West scarp crew. Six-year contract, came in on weight in four. I was on it, I took the early bonus and I spent it, and I'm not going to tell you I didn't.
My wife was born three doors up from where we live now. So we stayed.
Second hour of my night. I've not seen this town in daylight since the spring.
Third hour nothing, fourth hour nothing. What goes in the margin is mostly Wispurr, and they are up once the winter cold comes. Fourteen in a night last winter, and not one since the thaw.
The page has stayed empty since. Ives calls it a census. He calls it a census at me. At four.
Whatever Bly told you. A jar and a half left, second week of the month.
Same three rooms, same two lamps. I am buying oil now at a rate I never used to, and there was a wick in my hand when you came through that door, because I trim my own.

The week is not out, so I could not yet tell you what it has cost me, and I will have the bill for it when it is. Bly has it that the vale is no darker than it was, and Bly has been in this vale two winters.
My shutters are open all night and my lamp's out. So if I get a Wispurr I'm keeping it in the shed, and that is settled.
It has to be winter, she says, and winter takes forever.
So you can put it to her when you're passing, and I'll leave the shed door on the latch. Then it's done and nobody has to keep on about it.
Cold-pressed, then strained through flannel, then strained again.
Four burns to the fill, and I would stand on four. Anything giving you less was strained the once and jarred while the oil was still warm, and you can taste that on the second burn.
The wick gauge matters more than the oil does, and mine is fourteen to the inch. Any finer will not draw and any coarser smokes.
The ground's thin up the vale and dark half the day. The flock does very well on it, and nobody believes that until they have seen the lambs.
Umbrat graze that ground alongside my sheep, and the Wispurr come hunting the Umbrat once the cold's in. Neither has ever had a lamb off me.
The lambs are carrying weight this year. Put a hand on one. So.
We cut marked stands and nothing else. The marks come down from the town.
Webvern in the tops over this stand, so we cut round those trees. Reason given is the silk pays better than the timber. Off the stand by dusk, and the reason given there is Duskstalk.
Two hours out at the start and two hours back at the end. That is in the terms, and I have the terms by me in writing if you want the wording.
The lid's off that crate — they come open on their own and the Carricrow know it.
Contract's shut, so I'm pulling cable and rail out. You can follow the cable runs the whole way up from the vent line, and I'll walk you up if you've a morning to give it.
There's a rail up top that four of us couldn't shift. It's still up there, and I have a go at it most mornings going past, on my own, which tells you how that goes.

The warden's up and down this scarp with a book under her arm, and I was on the crew that worked it, right to the end. Quiet in the middle of the day, and it ought to be. It's quiet at dusk as well now, and it never used to be.
First time up here? There's a kettle on at the hut, and I'll not be offended if you walk straight past it.
More Carricrow than there used to be, and there were Stonewing lifting off that rock when I started.
The nest on the west scarp is empty, and I go past it every time I'm up for the rail. Nothing on it, nothing round it, and the white streak underneath has gone grey.
Stand off the east side while I'm reading. That's the town's lamps in the glass again.
I am out here rather than in the town, because in the town you are looking through the lamps all night.
The vale goes dark at about a degree a decade. That is the rate, and the chart gives the rate and no reason for it.
My figure for the day is nought. Company scout, posted here at first light to write down what comes back down.
The approach took six teams at first light and it is past noon.
Written out longhand. n, o, u, g, h, t. The people I report to would not want this said out loud. That gate was already open when we got here, and I have gone and said it, and I am going to stop now.

Every beast on the place gets a year older at the turn, whether it's been out on the grass all year or shut in the byre since the spring. We always brought ours down off the Reach the fortnight before.
The year goes over when the season's out. The lanterns are up on the green.
The festival goes on the water here. Every boat lit at once.
The whole channel goes orange and then the year turns. Corbett sets the price and we wait on the steps for the number the town eats on. The dry end of the steps goes first, so we get down early.
I pack stone round them and they still shift.
Three posts down the west end won't hold now. They're in the holes I dug six years ago. Ground's gone soft at that end since.
Every net I've cut down hangs in the shed on its own peg, oldest at the back. In the dark I can put my hand on the one I cut the year my son was born.
Three re-cuts in six years, and I overdid the second.
Picking's better than it ever was. Two more baskets out of that rise before dark, if the light holds.
Six years of the same four miles, and the Nibbin graze that rise flatter every year of it. Wet springs, I'd have said, and I only see it the one week.

Station's open, come in. This morning's numbers are up on the board, and the Reach column is the only one I've walked this week. What is under it has not been walked since last month, and I have marked those columns as last month.

The board goes under one arm and I'm out along the stilts most days this season. Four hours out of a day is what I get on those pages before the damp is into them. After that the pencil stops taking and I am walking for nothing.
Bowerdeep is slow ground for me. I'm on the forest floor with a glass looking up. That gets me about a third of the canopy, and I write the third down and mark it as a third.
Steppe survey, and I'm behind on it. Read over my shoulder if you like.
Shelves in the morning, out in the vale from dusk. The things I'm after are up and moving then. That gives me about four hours before the light comes back.
I'm up at the rim most of the day with the board. The only thing living on this approach is crows, and crows are what I'm counting.
Not seen a Fenmaw on the channel run all this season.
I used to put two a month in the back of my fare book. Now the Mirefin are right up under the boat. I put the pole down on one this morning, and I never meant to do it.
